newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to dismiss top Russian general.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to dismiss top Russian general.

text.p: The commander of Russia's land forces faced the sack on Monday for "actions incompatible with his post" but the Kremlin said President Boris Yeltsin had yet to sign the order dismissing him.
General Vladimir Semyonov, 56, said he was stunned by the news and denied any wrongdoing.

He told Izvestia newspaper he had been called in by Defence Minister Igor Rodionov on Friday evening and told he was being sacked because of serious allegations about unspecified "commercial activities" of his wife, who works in the Moscow office of Rosvertol, a Russian helicopter manufacturer.
The defence ministry said Semyonov was sacked "for actions which discredit the honour and dignity of a serviceman and are incompatible with his post".
But later a Kremlin statement said the the dismissal order had yet to be signed, though it made clear Yeltsin "agreed in principle" with it.
The presidential press service said the ministry had jumped the gun by presenting the sacking as a fait accompli when it had not yet been formalised.

"This is wholly unexpected," Interfax news agency quoted Semyonov as saying. "I have not received any concrete and convincing accusations from the defence minister and the reasons for my dismissal remain for me unclear."
He said he would fight to clear his name, but two former army generals now in parliament gave him little sympathy.

"Even if he did nothing discreditable he had to go. I think that this is one of the achievements of Rodionov, that the departure of those whom the army no longer needs is continuing," said Lev Rokhlin, chairman of the Duma defence committee.
Another member of the committee, former general Eduard Vorobyov, accused Semyonov of helping cover up the army's failure to carry out reforms.

The Russian media have published several articles over alleged corruption in the army top ranks but all those named have denied the allegations. Izvestia quoted the general as saying he planned to go to court to clear his name.
Interfax quoted military prosecutors as saying Semyonov did not figure among several high-ranking officers currently under official investigation.
"We have no materials concerning V. Semyonov that could serve as a reason for his dismissal," Interfax quoted a prosecution office source as saying.
Once the pride of Soviet society, the army has seen morale plummet in recent years amid acute cash shortages and humiliation at the hands of separatists in Chechnya.
Rodionov, appointed in July on the recommendation of now ousted security supremo Alexander Lebed, has shown an uncertain political touch and has yet to impose his authority in the top ranks.
He has made contradictory statements about the risk of a military revolt over the armed forces' problems, including shortages of equipment and supplies and unpaid wages.
Semyonov was appointed commander of Soviet ground forces in 1991 after the dismissal of General Valentin Varennikov, a supporter of the unsuccessful coup against President Mikhail Gorbachev.

The following year, after the superpower collapsed and its armed forces were divided, he was appointed chief of Russian land forces. In June 1996 he was promoted to the rank of army general, the equivalent of four-star general.
